subject: Psychology
topic: Operational definitions, experimental control and inference
scope: Original academic research-methods examples, not clinical advice or instructions to run human-subject experiments. Actual research requires appropriate ethical oversight.
prerequisites: Distinguish a claim from supporting evidence.
Interpret a mean and a comparison between groups.
objectives: Translate a broad construct into an operational measure.
Distinguish random assignment from random sampling.
Evaluate causal inference, validity and ethical limitations.

notes.heading: From constructs to measurements
paragraphs: Psychological constructs such as memory, attention or confidence are not identical to any one measurement. An operational definition specifies how a variable is manipulated or measured in a particular study. Counting correctly recalled words after a delay is one possible memory measure; it does not capture every form of memory. A useful definition makes procedures interpretable and repeatable while acknowledging the part of the construct it leaves out. Distinguish a hypothesis about a relationship from the particular task chosen to test it. A convenient measure is not automatically a valid measure of the intended construct.

notes.heading: Control and assignment
paragraphs: In an experiment, a researcher manipulates an independent variable and measures a dependent variable while trying to control alternative explanations. A confounding variable changes systematically with the manipulation and could explain the observed outcome. Random assignment allocates recruited participants to conditions and can reduce systematic pre-existing differences between those conditions. Random sampling concerns how participants are selected from a population; it addresses a different question about representativeness. Neither procedure guarantees that every small sample is perfectly balanced. Describe what was randomised rather than using random as a general synonym for fair.

notes.heading: Reliability and validity
paragraphs: Reliability concerns consistency of a measurement or procedure under relevant conditions. Validity concerns whether an interpretation or use is justified, including whether the measure captures the intended construct. A consistently miscalibrated scale illustrates how consistency can coexist with inaccuracy. Internal validity concerns whether an observed effect can be attributed to the proposed cause within the study; generalising beyond the study raises additional questions about people, settings, tasks and time. Correlation alone does not establish direction of causation or eliminate a common cause. A statistically clear pattern can still have a weak measurement or an unrepresentative sample.

notes.heading: Ethics and conclusions
paragraphs: Research involving people requires attention to informed participation, privacy, potential harm and the ability to withdraw under the applicable ethical framework. A classroom hypothetical design is not permission to carry out a real study. Ethical safeguards also affect interpretation: participants' expectations and the way a task is presented may influence behaviour. A conclusion should name the measured outcome and the conditions under which it was observed, rather than replacing a narrow result with a claim about every aspect of human behaviour. Evaluation is strongest when it explains how a specific design limitation could change the result and proposes a feasible, ethically appropriate way to investigate that uncertainty.

notes.heading: Separating random allocation from representative recruitment
paragraphs: Recruitment determines who enters a study; allocation determines which condition each recruited participant receives. Random allocation can reduce systematic differences between conditions, but it does not make a convenience sample representative of a wider population. Keep internal comparisons and generalisation separate when evaluating a study. Also operationalise the outcome: a score on a specified recall task is not every aspect of memory. If a fictional study uses volunteers from one club, describe that restriction instead of assuming all learners respond alike. Replication with different participants and settings can investigate generality. The example is a design exercise, not a report of a conducted experiment.

workedExamples.prompt: A study defines memory as the number of words recalled after ten minutes. Identify the operational measure and a limitation.
steps: The observed variable is the count of recalled words after the specified delay.
Other forms of memory and other delays are not directly measured.
workedExamples.answer: A delayed word-recall score operationalises one aspect of memory, not memory in every context.

workedExamples.prompt: Volunteers are randomly allocated to two instruction conditions. Does this make the sample representative of all students?
steps: Random allocation concerns conditions after recruitment.
Volunteer characteristics may differ from those of the wider population.
workedExamples.answer: No. Random assignment and representative population sampling are different design features.

workedExamples.prompt: A study finds that more reported stress accompanies fewer reported hours of sleep. Explain the causal limitation.
steps: The result is an association between two measures.
Either direction of influence or a third factor could contribute.
The association alone does not identify a unique causal mechanism.
workedExamples.answer: The relationship does not by itself establish which variable causes the other.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional study recruits 20 volunteers from one chess club, then randomly assigns 10 to quiet study and 10 to background music. Explain one benefit of allocation and one recruitment limitation.
workedExamples.answer: Random allocation can reduce systematic group differences; the club volunteer sample may not represent the wider learner population.
steps: Condition assignment is random among the recruited participants.
This helps distribute participant characteristics between conditions without guaranteeing perfect balance.
Recruitment from one self-selected club limits population generalisation.

misconceptions.claim: Random assignment guarantees a representative sample.
misconceptions.correction: Assignment allocates participants to conditions; sampling determines who enters the study.

misconceptions.claim: A reliable measure is automatically valid for every purpose.
misconceptions.correction: Consistency alone does not establish that the intended construct or interpretation is captured.

flashcards.front: What does an operational definition specify?
flashcards.back: How a variable is measured or manipulated in the particular study.

flashcards.front: What makes a variable a possible confound?
flashcards.back: It varies systematically with the proposed cause and offers an alternative explanation of the outcome.

flashcards.front: What question does random assignment address?
flashcards.back: How recruited participants are allocated to conditions, helping reduce systematic group differences.
How the participants are selected from the population of interest.

flashcards.front: Why can a consistent measure still be unsuitable?
flashcards.back: It may reliably measure something other than the intended construct.

flashcards.front: Name two alternatives to a claimed direction of causation in a correlation.
flashcards.back: Reverse direction and a common third cause.
Assignment of recruited participants to conditions; it can reduce systematic group differences.
No. Representativeness depends on recruitment, the sampling frame and participation patterns.

questions.prompt: Which procedure allocates already recruited participants to conditions?
options: A definition of the target population
solution: The participants have already been recruited.
The question concerns allocation between conditions.

questions.prompt: Give an operational measure for performance on a fixed ten-question recall task and one limit of that measure.
questions.answer: Count correct responses out of ten under the stated task conditions. This measures performance on that task, not every aspect of memory.
solution: Separate the measured task from the broader construct.

questions.prompt: Why might testing one instruction condition in the morning and the other late at night create a confound?
questions.answer: Time of day changes systematically with condition and could affect performance, so differences cannot be attributed uniquely to the instructions.
solution: Identify the variable changing alongside the instruction condition.
Explain its possible alternative influence on the measured result.
markingPoints: Identify time of day as a potential confound.
Link it to the uncertainty in causal attribution.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim that an association between revision time and examination marks proves that extra revision causes higher marks.
questions.answer: The association is compatible with a causal effect, but motivation, prior knowledge or other factors could influence both variables. The observational relationship alone does not isolate the effect of changing revision time.
solution: Limit the causal conclusion to what the design supports.

questions.prompt: A self-report questionnaire gives similar scores a week apart. What can and cannot be concluded about the instrument?
questions.answer: The result supports consistency over that interval in that sample. It does not alone establish construct validity, freedom from response bias or applicability to different populations.
solution: State that validity requires additional justification.
Limit generalisation to the tested conditions and sample.

questions.prompt: A fictional study recruits 20 volunteers from one chess club, then randomly assigns 10 to quiet study and 10 to background music. Explain one benefit of allocation and one recruitment limitation.
questions.answer: Random allocation can reduce systematic group differences; the club volunteer sample may not represent the wider learner population.
solution: Condition assignment is random among the recruited participants.
This helps distribute participant characteristics between conditions without guaranteeing perfect balance.
Recruitment from one self-selected club limits population generalisation.
markingPoints: Condition assignment is random among the recruited participants.
This helps distribute participant characteristics between conditions without guaranteeing perfect balance.
Recruitment from one self-selected club limits population generalisation.

questions.prompt: A learner says random allocation proves the sample represents all teenagers. Correct the terminology and suggest a recruitment improvement.
questions.answer: Random allocation concerns conditions, not population sampling. Recruit from a broader defined sampling frame using a justified sampling method.
solution: Distinguish recruitment into the study from assignment within it.
The original participants still come only from one volunteer club.
Broader recruitment can address coverage, though response bias and other limits still need reporting.
markingPoints: Distinguish recruitment into the study from assignment within it.
The original participants still come only from one volunteer club.
Broader recruitment can address coverage, though response bias and other limits still need reporting.
